title: Stream congestion & launch-rate effects across cloud GPU SKUs
content:
Summary:
This exploratory document records a focused sweep investigating how CPU-side launch rates, concurrent CUDA stream counts, and driver/CUDA combinations affect micro-batch small-token inference latency and tail-behavior across representative cloud SKUs (A100, H100, L40S). The goal is practical: identify safe concurrency knobs for our serving runtime that improve throughput without regressing p95/p99 and to flag driver/OS combinations that introduce hidden launch throttling or serialization.

Why this matters:
- Our production mix is dominated by low token-per-request (1-8) inference; optimizing for large-batch throughput misses common cases.
- Overlap (H2D/D2H + kernel compute) and multi-stream execution are key levers, but they interact with driver-level limits (launch throughput), PCIe/NVLink characteristics, and host-side burst handling.
- We observed occasional p99 spikes in canaries that correlated with bursts of tiny kernels; this doc is the systematic chase.

Concrete questions we tried to answer:
1) For small per-request kernels (~200800 us total kernel time split across several ops), what stream counts maximize sustained tokens/sec while keeping p99 within SLO?
2) Do different SKUs (p4d A100, p5 H100, GCP L40S) exhibit different sweet-spots for streams and memcpy overlap?
3) Are there driver or CUDA combos where CPU launcher becomes the bottleneck (observed as serialized invocation patterns or launch latency growth under burst)?
4) Any obvious mitigations (pinning, batching, host-side rate-limit, CUDA Graph warmup) that are low-cost to implement?

Test matrix (concise):
- SKUs tested: AWS p4d (A100-80GB), AWS p5 (H100-80GB), GCP L40S (L40S) -- single-GPU instances pinned to same region where possible.
- Drivers/CUDA: CUDA 11.8 w/ driver 535, CUDA 12.1 w/ driver 550, CUDA 12.2 experimental (where available on H100).
- OS: Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 variants (noted per run).
- Workload: synthetic inference harness that simulates our token-gen pipeline: tiny forward kernels, KV-cache memcpy patterns, small softmax/linear kernels. Micro-batch sizes: 1, 2, 4. Sequence context: 128 tokens.
- Concurrency knobs: concurrent streams = [1,2,4,8,16], host launcher threads = [1,2,4], pinned vs non-pinned host memory for H2D, and CUDA Graph warmup enabled/disabled.
- Measurement: steady-state tokens/sec (60s windows after warmup), p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per token, kernel launch rate (launches/sec), CPU-side wakeups, and memcpy overlap efficiency (time saved vs no overlap).

Methodology notes and instrumentation:
- Used per-kernel timestamps via CUPTI where available; fallback to nvtx + event timing when CUPTI not present.
- Captured host perf counters for context-switches and syscalls to detect host-side throttling when launch burst increases.
- Runs repeated 5x, report median unless distribution shows multimodality.
- Where CUDA Graph warmup used, we replayed the graph 200x prior to measurement.

Key findings (summary):
- H100 (p5) generally tolerates higher concurrent streams (4) for our micro-kernels, achieving better tokens/sec and lower p95 than single-stream with pinned memory overlap enabled. p99 improved modestly but occasionally regressed when using >8 streams due to scheduler fragmentation.
- A100 (p4d) performed well up to 2 streams; beyond that we saw diminishing returns and in some driver combos (CUDA 11.8 + driver 535) clear signs of CPU-side launch slowdown manifested as a growing inter-launch latency under sustained bursts. Upgrading to CUDA 12.1/driver 550 reduced that effect.
- L40S (GCP) provided competitive single-stream latency but showed weaker memcpy+compute overlap: measured H2D overlap savings were 30% lower than H100 for equivalent pinned-memory runs. Multi-stream concurrency above 4 often increased p99.
- CUDA Graph warmup consistently reduced p50 and p90 and eliminated a portion of CPU launch overhead for single-pattern execution. It was most effective on A100 where it masked some old-driver launch penalties.

Concrete numbers (representative run, micro-batch=1, seq=128):
- H100, CUDA12.1: 4 streams, pinned H2D -> tokens/sec +18% vs 1 stream; p95 -12% (improved). p99 -5% (improved) with 4 streams; 8 streams -> p99 regressed +22% in 1/5 runs.
- A100, CUDA11.8: 2 streams, non-pinned -> tokens/sec +6%; 8 streams -> launch-rate stalled, p99 +45% (bad). After driver 550 upgrade: 8 streams behaved much better, tokens/sec +12% and p99 within 10% of baseline.
- L40S, CUDA12.1: 2 streams best tradeoff; pinned memory helped but overlap effectiveness lower vs H100 (~60% of H100 overlap savings).

Observations and diagnostic artifacts:
- Host CPU wakeups and context-switch counts correlated with launch-rate saturation. In A100 older driver runs, the host process saw increased syscall latency when launches/sec exceeded ~18k, which matched a drop in sustained kernel parallelism.
- NVLink vs PCIe behavior: H100 maintained higher effective overlap due to multi-path memory fabric; L40S (PCIe-bound in our tests) had less tolerance for concurrent H2D.
- Some cloud images had driver packaging that mismatched kernel modules vs toolkit version; noisy results flagged where kernel/driver mismatch warnings appeared in dmesg.

Practical recommendations (engineer-facing):
1) Default to 2 streams for A100 in production unless we pin driver/toolkit to CUDA12.1+ and validate via a short canary that 4 streams are safe for that image.
2) For H100, use 4 streams as the sweet-spot for small-token workloads, but cap at 6 in autoscaling configs to avoid scheduler fragmentation on noisy hosts.
3) L40S: prefer single/dual-stream with pinned H2D where possible; avoid >4 concurrent streams in default configs.
4) Implement optional CUDA Graph warmup path for steady-pattern inference (cheap and reduces p50/p90).
5) Add a lightweight host-side launch-rate monitor to canaries (detect sustained launches/sec > threshold and emit an alert or fallback to single-threaded launcher).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Re-run a focused set with NVSwitch-enabled H100 multi-GPU to see if fragmentation trends persist when multiple GPUs share fabric.
- Test on newer driver rollouts (post-550) across cloud images to build a recommended matrix for infra infra/ami/packer images.
- Integrate a small microbenchmark into our CI that reproduces the launch-rate saturation pattern to catch regressions.

Experiment logs (short):
- 2024-09-18: initial sweep A100/CUDA11.8 showed launch stall. Logged CUPTI traces and host perf.
- 2024-09-25: H100 CUDA12.1 runs, found 4-stream sweet spot.
- 2024-10-02: GCP L40S runs, discovered weaker overlap, repeated with pinned vs non-pinned; pinned better but still lower savings.
- 2024-10-20: validation after driver 550 image baked, A100 improved.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an exploratory, not exhaustive study. Results are sensitive to cloud image/driver packaging and host OS.
- If we decide to operationalize any of these knobs, we must add image-level metadata to our deployment manifests indicating validated drivers/CUDA.
- Many of the mitigations (CUDA Graph, pinned memory) are low-cost to apply in our serving codepath; I recommend small follow-up PRs to add optional toggles behind the runtime config.

Attachments / useful artifacts (links above): CUPTI traces, perf scripts, sanity dashboards (linked in linked_artifacts).
